You asked me, 'Binita, when did you first notice?' Honestly, it was small things. My brother Divyansh used to call me every Sunday from his college hostel. Then it was every other Sunday. Then he'd say, 'Can't talk, I'm at the centre.'
When he came home at Holi, he used words I didn't know. 'Awake ones.' 'Noise people.' He called his old school friends noise people. He'd stopped replying to them.
I asked about his exams. He said he'd dropped two papers because 'the real learning is at the centre now'. When Papa asked a question about the fees, Divyansh said, very calmly, 'Only the guide's word is true. Questions are a test of loyalty. People who ask too many get asked to sit out of the circle.'
Then he told me, gently, that maybe I should give him some space. That family can be a distraction.
That's when I got scared. That's why I'm talking to you.

Asif, you asked how your old neighbour Ramesh knew something was wrong with my brother Mohan, back when I was your age. It wasn't one thing. It was many small ones.
Mohan was nineteen, studying at the polytechnic. First he started using words that weren't ours: "the awakened", "sleepers". Then he stopped writing to his school friends. When our mother asked about his exams, he said the leader had told them studies were for sleepers. He quoted that man about everything, as if nobody else in the world had ever had a thought.
One day he told me a friend had been made to stand outside the hall all night for asking where the donations went. He said it proudly.
I was angry. I wanted to shake him. But he was still my little brother. So I kept writing to him every week, about nothing: cricket, Amma's cooking. It was a year before he wrote back properly. But he did.

qa.a: At the polytechnic.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when Mohan told the story of the punishment proudly?
qa.a: Ramesh felt angry and frightened for Mohan, but also tender, because Mohan was still a little brother.

qa.a: Instead of shaking or scolding Mohan, Ramesh kept writing weekly letters about ordinary things, keeping the bond open.

qa.a: Mohan saw it as right and even something to be proud of, a sign of how far the group's control had shaped his view.

Rehana worked night shifts as a nurse in Muscat, so she saw her daughter Alka only as a small face on a video call every Sunday morning. Lately that face had changed.
Alka had stopped mentioning her college friends. She talked instead about "the Circle" and used strange phrases: "clean thinking", "outside noise". When Rehana asked about her semester marks, Alka said she had paused college because "the Circle needs builders now".
Last Sunday Alka whispered that members who asked too many questions were "put on pause" and nobody spoke to them. Then: "Ammi, maybe we should talk less. You're outside noise too."
Rehana hung up, heart pounding. She couldn't fly home for two months. So she wrote down the signs: one voice for truth, penalties for questions, pressure to cut off family. Then she called her sister in Pune and asked her to visit Alka that very afternoon, just for lunch.
